title: Formation of the Earth
tagline: How the Earth condensed from a cloud of gas, differentiated into layers, and acquired the structure that governs everything that happens on its surface.

overview.intro: The Earth is about 4.5 billion years old, and its present form is the outcome of condensation from a rotating cloud of gas and dust, followed by internal differentiation into core, mantle and crust. That history matters because it explains why the planet is layered, why it is warm inside, why its surface is restless, and why water and an atmosphere could survive on it. This unit covers the nebular hypothesis and the stages of Earth formation, the interior structure and the evidence for it, the layers of the atmosphere, and the surface features shaped by internal and external forces.

learn.title: The nebular hypothesis and stages of Earth formation

blocks.text: The nebular hypothesis, developed by Kant and Laplace, holds that the solar system condensed from a rotating cloud of gas and dust called the solar nebula. As the cloud cooled, material began to condense around the centre, and the rotating disc flattened into a ring-shaped structure with a dense, hot sphere at the centre that became the Sun. Within the disc, dust grains collided and stuck together to form progressively larger bodies, ending with planetesimals and finally planets. Because the whole disc rotated in one direction, the planets revolve in the same direction and roughly the same plane.

blocks.caption: Stages in the formation of the Earth
rows: A rotating cloud of hydrogen, helium and dust begins to cool
Rotation flattens the cloud into a disc with a dense centre
Dust accretes into grains, pebbles, then planetesimals
Heavier iron and nickel sink inward; lighter silicates rise outward
Outgassing and cooling form a solid crust and a primitive atmosphere
Water vapour condenses as the surface cools below 100 degrees Celsius

items: The Earth was initially hot and molten, which allowed materials to separate by density.
Radioactive decay and continued impacts kept the interior hot.
The crust solidified first while the interior remained plastic.
Outgassing from the interior produced the early atmosphere and water vapour.
Differentiation produced the dense metallic core and the lighter rocky mantle and crust.

learn.title: The interior of the Earth and the evidence for it

blocks.text: The interior is divided into the crust, the mantle and the core. The crust is the thin, solid outer layer, of two kinds: light granitic continental crust up to about 35 kilometres thick, and denser basaltic oceanic crust of about 5 to 10 kilometres. Beneath it lies the mantle, about 2,900 kilometres thick, of which the upper portion is partially molten and from which magma rises. At the centre is the core, largely iron and nickel, with a liquid outer core and a solid inner core kept solid by enormous pressure.

Direct observation is impossible below the deepest mines and boreholes, so the evidence is indirect. Seismic waves are the principal tool: primary or P waves travel through solids and liquids, while secondary or S waves cannot pass through liquids, and their behaviour reveals which layers are solid. Reflection and refraction of waves at boundaries identify the discontinuities, including the Gutenberg discontinuity between mantle and core and the Mohorovicic discontinuity between crust and mantle. Gravity measurements, the Earth’s magnetic field and heat flow from the interior provide supporting evidence.

blocks.caption: Layers of the Earth with their state and thickness
rows: 5–10 km oceanic, up to 35 km continental
Part of a mantle about 2,900 km thick
Rigid, with a plastic asthenosphere below
Liquid iron and nickel, source of the magnetic field
Solid iron and nickel under extreme pressure

items.text: S waves vanish at the core boundary on the far side of the Earth.
items.note: Their disappearance shows the outer core is liquid, since shear waves cannot pass through a liquid.

items.text: Continental crust is much thicker than oceanic crust yet less dense.
items.note: That is why continents stand high and ocean basins stay low, and why one can be subducted under the other.

learn.title: Internal and external forces shaping the surface

blocks.text: The surface of the Earth is shaped by two opposing families of forces. Internal or endogenic forces originate within the Earth: convection in the mantle drives plate movement, volcanism builds new land, and folding and faulting crumple or fracture crustal rock to build mountains. External or exogenic forces act on the surface from outside: weathering breaks rock in place, erosion removes and transports the debris, and deposition lays it down again, while running water, wind, glaciers and waves each sculpt characteristic landforms. Internal forces raise relief and external forces level it, and the present landscape records the balance between them at any moment.

blocks.caption: Internal against external forces
rows: Heat from within, mantle convection, gravity
Solar energy driving wind, water and ice
Fold mountains, rift valleys, volcanic islands

items: Epeirogenic movements are broad, gentle uplift or subsidence of large areas.
Orogenic movements are violent and produce mountain-building by folding.
Weathering prepares rock for removal by breaking it in place.
Erosion is the combined action of weathering, detachment and transport.
The grade, or equilibrium slope, is what a river works toward over time.

learn.title: Why formation and structure matter for the surface

blocks.text: The Earth’s internal heat, inherited from its formation and renewed by radioactive decay, drives mantle convection and therefore plate tectonics, which in turn controls where mountains rise, where volcanoes erupt and where ocean basins open. The cooling that produced a solid crust also allowed an atmosphere of nitrogen and oxygen to persist and liquid water to remain on the surface, because a planet of this mass holds gases that a smaller body would have lost. The layered structure thus sets the stage: the crust supplies the material, the mantle supplies the energy, and the atmosphere and hydrosphere supply the agents of external wear.

items.text: Continental drift explains why matching fossils appear on separated continents.
items.note: The fragments were once joined, which shows that the surface has been rearranged by internal forces.

items.text: A volcano building an island while waves attack its flanks.
items.note: Internal construction and external destruction operating on the same landform at the same time.

keyPoints: The Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago from the solar nebula.
The nebular hypothesis explains the common direction and plane of planetary orbits.
Differentiation of a molten Earth produced a dense core, a mantle and a light crust.
The interior is crust, mantle, outer core and inner core.
Seismic waves are the main evidence: S waves cannot pass through liquids.
The liquid outer core is the source of the Earth’s magnetic field.
Endogenic forces build relief through folding, faulting and volcanism.
Exogenic forces reduce relief through weathering, erosion and deposition.
Continental crust is thicker and lighter than oceanic crust.
Internal heat from formation and radioactive decay drives plate movement.
examFocus: Formation questions want the stages in order, each with a line of what changed.
Interior answers should name the evidence, since direct observation is impossible and marks are for the indirect reasoning.
Landform questions earn marks by attributing each feature to internal or external action before describing it.

questions.prompt: The nebular hypothesis explains the formation of the Earth from:
options: A cloud of gas and dust that condensed and rotated
Molten rock expelled by another planet
Ice that accumulated in the outer solar system
Debris left by a passing star
questions.answer: A cloud of gas and dust that condensed and rotated
questions.explanation: The solar nebula cooled and condensed while rotating, flattening into a disc from which the planets accreted.

questions.prompt: Which layer of the Earth is liquid at ordinary conditions?
questions.explanation: The outer core is liquid iron and nickel, and its motion generates the Earth’s magnetic field.

questions.prompt: The evidence that the outer core is liquid comes chiefly from:
options: S waves not passing through it
questions.answer: S waves not passing through it
questions.explanation: Secondary waves are shear waves and cannot travel through a liquid, so their disappearance marks a liquid layer.

questions.prompt: A fold mountain range is built mainly by:
options: Endogenic forces of compression in the crust
questions.answer: Endogenic forces of compression in the crust
questions.explanation: Compression in the crust folds sedimentary beds upward, which is an internal force acting on rock that external forces later sculpt.

questions.prompt: The thin, solid outer layer of the Earth, continental or oceanic, is called the __________ .
questions.explanation: Continental crust is thicker and lighter while oceanic crust is thinner and denser, which is why continents stand above the ocean basins.

questions.prompt: The separation of Earth’s materials by density while the planet was molten is called __________ .
questions.explanation: Heavy iron and nickel sank to form the core while lighter silicates rose to form mantle and crust.

questions.prompt: State four stages in the formation of the Earth.
questions.answer: Four stages are: the cooling and rotation of the solar nebula of gas and dust; flattening of the cloud into a disc with a dense centre; accretion of dust into grains, planetesimals and finally the Earth; and differentiation of the molten planet by density into core, mantle and crust. Outgassing to form an early atmosphere and the condensation of oceans are also accepted.
questions.explanation: Stages must be in a defensible sequence with a line of explanation each, not a bare list of names.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between endogenic and exogenic forces on three bases.
questions.answer: On source, endogenic forces come from heat and gravity within the Earth while exogenic forces are driven by solar energy acting on the surface. On action, endogenic forces fold, fault and erupt, while exogenic forces weather, erode, transport and deposit. On effect, endogenic forces build relief such as mountains and plateaus, while exogenic forces reduce it to valleys, plains and deltas. The speed also differs, since endogenic events are often sudden whereas exogenic work is slow and continuous.
questions.explanation: Three bases of comparison are required, each drawn as a contrast rather than a description of one set of forces.

questions.prompt: Describe the interior of the Earth and explain how it is known.
questions.answer: The interior consists of the crust, the mantle and the core. The crust is the thin solid outer layer, granitic and up to 35 kilometres thick beneath continents and basaltic and about 5 to 10 kilometres thick beneath the oceans. Below it lies the mantle, roughly 2,900 kilometres thick, whose upper part is partially molten and supplies magma, with a plastic asthenosphere on which the rigid plates move. The core is about 3,470 kilometres in radius and is largely iron and nickel, with a liquid outer core and a solid inner core held solid by pressure. Knowledge of this structure is indirect. Seismic waves are the principal tool: P waves pass through solids and liquids while S waves cannot pass through liquids, so the disappearance of S waves at the core boundary proves the outer core is liquid. Reflection and refraction of waves at boundaries identify the Gutenberg and Mohorovicic discontinuities, and gravity measurements, heat flow and the Earth’s magnetic field supply supporting evidence.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the layers with their state and the reasoning by which each is inferred, since no borehole reaches below a few kilometres.

questions.prompt: Explain how the Earth’s formation explains why it is layered, why it is still geologically active, and why it can hold liquid water and an atmosphere.
questions.answer: The layered structure follows directly from formation: the young Earth was hot and molten, so gravity separated its materials by density, iron and nickel sinking to the core while lighter silicates rose to form the mantle and crust. That process, called differentiation, is why the planet has a dense centre and a light surface rather than a uniform composition. Continued geological activity also follows from formation: heat trapped during accretion was supplemented by radioactive decay, and that internal heat drives convection in the mantle, which moves the plates, builds mountains, feeds volcanoes and causes earthquakes. The capacity to hold water and air follows from the combination of a cooling surface and sufficient mass: as the crust solidified, outgassing produced an atmosphere of carbon dioxide, nitrogen and water vapour, and once the surface cooled below 100 degrees the water vapour condensed into oceans, while the Earth’s gravity was large enough to retain those gases. The present surface is therefore the visible product of heat and material inherited from the planet’s origin.
questions.explanation: The answer is marked on connecting three effects back to the single cause of formation and differentiation, rather than treating them as unrelated facts.
